sentences.text: Galveosaurus herreroi is the sole species of an extinct macronarian sauropod that lived roughly 147 million years ago during the Late Jurassic in Europe.
This dinosaur resembles earlier forms like Cetiosaurus and Barapasaurus but represents a more advanced evolutionary stage.
It was a medium-sized sauropod reaching 16 meters in length, standing 4 meters tall, and weighing approximately 9 tonnes.
The animal appears to have kept many primitive traits while evolving along a distinct path separate from other sauropod groups.
The fossil record contains unique elements such as a sternum plate, a chevron, and fragments of ribs alongside standard limb bones.
The specific epithet herreroi honors the amateur fossil hunter who first found the remains.
Local amateur fossil hunter José María Herrero discovered the remains at the Cuesta Lonsal site near Galve, Spain, during the 1980s.
Excavations at this location in Teruel, Spain, were conducted by Herrero during that decade.
Between 1993 and 2002, researchers recovered over 50 associated bones belonging to this new sauropod species.
The bones were found in the Villar del Arzobispo Formation, which provided the origin for the genus name.
The name Galveosaurus herreroi was first published in an article by Bárbara Sánchez-Hernández on August 11, 2005.
A separate team led by Barco et al. later described the animal as Galvesaurus herreroi, omitting the letter 'o' in the genus name.
After preparation and study, the fossil bones were moved to the Spanish Paleontological Museum of Galve for public display.
As the remains underwent preparation and study, the team transferred them to the small Paleontological Museum of Galve for exhibition.
The parent group of this dinosaur is Macronaria.
Galveosaurus belongs to the class Saurischia.
While Royo-Torres et al. (2006) placed it within Turiasauria, Barco and Canudo (2012) showed it lacks Turiasauria synapomorphies and is actually a macronarian.
A 2024 phylogenetic analysis recovered Galvesaurus as a sister taxon of Titanosauriformes outside Brachiosauridae.
In the Villar del Arzobispo Formation, bones and tracks of other sauropods, theropods, and ornithopods have been found alongside remains of this species.
The sauropod Losillasaurus was discovered only 80 km from Galve and is of an age close to that of Galveosaurus.
The Aragosaurus team disputed the validity of the name Galveosaurus, arguing that their publication date of July 1, 2005, was valid within the journal's July–December 2005 range.
Sánchez-Hernández argued that the publication date for Barco et al. is technically December 31, 2005, citing ICZN articles 21.6 and 23, making her name valid.
The Aragosaurus team alleged that Sánchez Hernández knew other scientists were working on the specimen and cited their previous research, suggesting unethical publication practices.
It is debated whether Sánchez Hernández had first-hand access to the specimen, with the Aragosaurus team claiming her photos showed the public display cabinet frame.
